      51             : // A representation of a set of DispatchKeys. A DispatchKeySet contains both
      52             : // "functionality" bits and "backend bits", and every tensor holds its own
      53             : // DispatchKeySet. The Dispatcher implements multiple dispatch by grabbing the
      54             : // keyset on every input tensor, or’ing them together, and dispatching to a
      55             : // specific piece of functionality. The functionality bits are *ordered*. When
      56             : // multiple functionality bits are set, we use the highest priority
      57             : // functionality. Similarly, multiple backend bits can theoretically be set if
      58             : // you call an operator with multiple tensors from difference devices (e.g. CPU
      59             : // and CUDA), although support for mixed device dispatch is limited (the only
      60             : // kernels that gracefully handle mixed device inputs for now are cuda kernels
      61             : // that take in a scalar cpu tensor).
      62             : 
      63             : // A representation of a set of DispatchKeys.  A tensor may have multiple
      64             : // tensor type ids, e.g., a Variable tensor can also be a CPU tensor; the
      65             : // DispatchKeySet specifies what type ids apply.  The internal representation is
      66             : // as a 64-bit bit set (this means only 64 tensor type ids are supported).
      67             : //
      68             : // As mentioned above, DispatchKeys are ordered; thus, we can ask questions like
      69             : // "what is the highest priority DispatchKey in the set"?  (The set itself is
      70             : // not ordered; two sets with the same ids will always have the ids ordered in
      71             : // the same way.)
      72             : //
      73             : // Note [DispatchKeySet Internal Representation]
      74             : // Internally, dispatch keys are packed into 64-bit DispatchKeySet objects
      75             : // that get passed around at runtime.
      76             : // However, there isn't necessarily a 1-to-1 mapping between bits in the keyset
      77             : // and individual dispatch keys.
      78             : //
      79             : // First: why do we have this distinction, and why not map every dispatch key
      80             : // directly to a bit? This is mostly because we have several types of
      81             : // functionalities that different backends would like to customize. For example,
      82             : // we have:
      83             : // - "Dense":     CPU, CUDA, XLA, ... (~12 keys)
      84             : // - "Sparse":    SparseCPU, SparseCUDA, ...
      85             : // - "SparseCsr": SparseCsrCPU, SparseCsrCUDA, ...
      86             : // - "Quantized": QuantizedCPU, QuantizedCUDA, QuantizedXLA, ...
      87             : // - "Autograd":  AutogradCPU, AutogradCUDA, Autograd XLA, ...
      88             : // The problem is that total number of keys grows quadratically with [#
      89             : // backends] x [# functionalities], making it very difficult to map each key
      90             : // directly to a bit in a bitset without dramatically increasing the size of the
      91             : // bitset over time.
      92             : //
      93             : // The two enums (BackendComponent and DispatchKey) can be divided roughly into
      94             : // 5 categories.
      95             : //
      96             : // (1) "Building block" keys
      97             : //    (a) backends: Everything in the BackendComponent enum (e.g. CPUBit,
      98             : //    CUDABit) (b) functionalities: (per-backend) functionality-bit DispatchKeys
      99             : //    (e.g. AutogradFunctionality, SparseCsr, Sparse, Dense)
     100             : // (2) "Runtime" keys
     101             : //    (a) "non-customizable backends" (e.g. FPGA)
     102             : //    (b) "non-customizable functionalities" (e.g. Functionalize)
     103             : //    (c) "per-backend instances of customizable functionalities" (e.g. CPU,
     104             : //    SparseCPU, AutogradCPU)
     105             : // (3) "Alias" DispatchKeys (see Note [Alias Dispatch Keys])
     106             : //
     107             : // (1) Building block keys always correspond to individual bits in a
     108             : // DispatchKeySet. They can also be combined in a DispatchKeySet to form actual
     109             : // runtime keys. e.g.
     110             : //     auto dense_cpu_ks = DispatchKeySet({DispatchKey::CPUBit,
     111             : //     DispatchKey::Dense});
     112             : //     // The keyset has the runtime dense-cpu key.
     113             : //     dense_cpu_ks.has(DispatchKey::CPU);
     114             : //     // And it contains the building block keys too.
     115             : //     dense_cpu_ks.has(DispatchKey::CPUBit);
     116             : //     dense_cpu_ks.has(DispatchKey::Dense);
     117             : //
     118             : // Not every backend and not every functionality counts as a "building block
     119             : // key". This is mostly to give us more levers to pull in the design space.
     120             : // Backend keys and functionality keys that count as "building blocks" will
     121             : // contribute to a full cross product of functionality that can be overridden.
     122             : //
     123             : // For example, right now we have at least 12 "backend" building
     124             : // blocks (CPU, CUDA, XLA, ...) and at least 5 "functionality"
     125             : // building blocks (Dense, Sparse, SparseCsr, Quantized,
     126             : // AutogradFunctionality, ...). These keys together allow every
     127             : // dispatcher operator to be customized in up to 12*4 different
     128             : // ways. Each of those requires a slot in the operator table of every
     129             : // dispatcher operator.  Not every piece of functionality necessarily
     130             : // needs to be customizable per-backend, and not every backend
     131             : // necessarily needs to be able to customize every type of
     132             : // functionality.
     133             : //
     134             : //
     135             : // (2) Every runtime key corresponds directly to a slot in an operator's runtime
     136             : // dispatch table, and you can directly register kernels to a runtime dispatch
     137             : // key.
     138             : //
     139             : // For per-backend functionalities like "Dense" or "AutogradFunctionality",
     140             : // you can think of the corresponding runtime dispatch keys as "instances" of
     141             : // that functionality, per backend. E.g. "CPU", "CUDA", "XLA", etc. are all
     142             : // runtime instances of the "Dense" building block key.
     143             : 
     144             : // (2a) and (2b) are represented identically in the DispatchKeySet logic:
     145             : // - backend-agnostic functionalities (e.g. FuncTorchBatched) are NOT
     146             : // customizable per backend.
     147             : //   In order to do so, we'd need to promote it to a per-backend functionality
     148             : //   "building block" key.
     149             : // - non-customizable backends (e.g. FPGA) can NOT customize existing
     150             : // functionality like Sparse, Autograd, etc.
     151             : //   In order to do so, we'd need to promote it to a backend "building block"
     152             : //   key.
     153             : //
     154             : // In both cases, these keys directly correspond to runtime slots in the
     155             : // operator table.
     156             : //
     157             : //
     158             : // (3) "Alias" keys
     159             : // See Note [Alias Dispatch Keys]
     160             : //
     161             : // Final note: for anyone making future changes to the Dispatcher +
     162             : // DispatchKeySet internals, there's a closed PR with a basic
     163             : // python-implementation of the Dispatcher that might be useful in quickly
     164             : // testing out and validating changes. See it at
     165             : // https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/68743
